strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and clearly articulated: in standard MLLMs, causal attention prevents image tokens from accessing the question text, and MMA is a minimal, parameter-free fix that unlocks this path. The formalization (Eqs. 2, 5, 6) is clean and the generalized form for interleaved/modalities is a nice touch.

The apples-to-apples evaluation is a decisive strength: MMA is compared against the standard (I&T)PT+(I&T)SFT pipeline, the SOTA anti-hallucination method CCA, and a newly introduced dual-order training (DOT) baseline plus four DOT variants, all under identical data, architecture, and training budgets (Table 1). MMA wins 11 of 12 benchmarks, often by large margins.

The DOT study is valuable in its own right, demonstrating that simply reordering modalities is insufficient and can be harmful, which strengthens the argument that architectural cross-modal visibility (rather than data ordering) is the key factor.

Reproducibility is well supported: hyperparameters (Table 3), sampling ratios (Table 4), per-dataset prompt templates (Tables 5, 6), compute details (8xA100, training durations), and detailed per-category benchmark scores (Appendix C) are all provided; code and the AKI-4B model are promised for release.

The limitations section is honest and precise: it clearly explains why MMA cannot be naively applied in the pretraining stage (information leakage through image tokens connecting future text tokens), which is an important and correctly identified constraint.
weaknesses: Originality is limited. The modification is a single attention-mask change, and the general idea of relaxing causal masks between modalities is conceptually close to prefix-LM-style masking and to CCA's mask manipulation (which the paper compares against). The paper would benefit from a deeper discussion of other bidirectional-attention variants in multimodal transformers and from experiments isolating e.g. which layers benefit from MMA.

The headline claim that AKI-4B achieves 'superior performance compared to both open-source and proprietary models of similar size across most benchmarks' (Introduction) is overstated. In Table 2, BLIP-3-4B outperforms AKI-4B on MMB (76.0 vs 73.1), SEED-I (71.8 vs 69.4), MMMU (40.1 vs 38.7), MM-Vet (41.0 vs 40.8), CV-Bench2D (66.2 vs 62.1), and CV-Bench3D (75.4 vs 71.8); AKI-4B wins only MMEP, MMEC, and LLaVAW. The SOTA claims should be substantially toned down.

There is no mechanistic analysis of why MMA works. Attention-map visualizations showing image tokens attending to question tokens, or ablations on partial unlocking (e.g., selected layers or token subsets), would greatly strengthen the causal story. As presented, the improvement could partly reflect prompt-conditioned vision features acting as a regularizer rather than genuine 'seeing' of the query.
Results are single-run with no variance estimates or significance testing; some headline gains (e.g., POPE at +1% over CCA, CV-Bench3D +2.1%) are within plausible run-to-run noise.

Presentation has noticeable errors: Table 8 lists AKI-4B's Relation Reasoning score as '0.65' (inconsistent formatting, apparently 65); the improvements row in Table 1 mixes percentage formats and has an ambiguous '-' entry; the abstract's '+7.2% average' is computed only relative to CCA, which should be stated more explicitly.
Generalization claims to audio, interleaved data, and hierarchical inputs (Eq. 6, Broader Impacts) are speculative and unsupported by any experiments.

strengths: The core idea (modality-mutual attention, MMA) is simple, parameter-free, and easy to implement: only the attention mask is changed so image tokens can attend to question tokens during SFT, making it trivially compatible with existing MLLM training pipelines.

The evaluation includes careful apples-to-apples comparisons under identical training configurations, datasets, and schedules, against a conventional causal pipeline, the state-of-the-art CCA baseline, and a well-motivated dual-order training (DOT) alternative, across 12 benchmarks spanning general, knowledge, and vision-centric categories.

The DOT experiments serve as a useful diagnostic: they empirically demonstrate that cross-modal information flow matters, and that naive order augmentation is inferior to MMA, strengthening the motivation for the proposed design.

The paper provides substantial implementation detail (hyperparameters, prompt templates, dataset statistics, sampling ratios, hardware), supporting reproducibility, and the limitation section honestly identifies the information-leakage problem that prevents applying MMA in the pretraining stage.
weaknesses: The claim that this perspective is 'fundamental yet unexplored' is overstated. Bidirectional/prefix-LM-style attention over image (and cross-modal) tokens has been used in prior multimodal architectures, and the design is a rather small modification of the attention mask; the delta over CCA [43], which already manipulates image-token attention masks, is incremental.

Mechanistic understanding is lacking. The paper asserts that letting image tokens attend to text tokens reduces hallucination, but provides no analysis of what the image tokens actually attend to (e.g., attention visualizations over question tokens), no probing of information flow, and no ablation of where in the network or how much the unlocked paths matter. The large gains (e.g., +29.5% on MME-C, +10.9% on MME-P) are reported without seeds, variance, or statistical significance, which is surprising for effects of this magnitude.

Several key claims are asserted but not tested: the generalization to interleaved/multi-modal inputs (Eq. 6) is unvalidated; the PT-stage leakage problem is acknowledged but no workaround (e.g., masking text-to-future-text leakage paths) is attempted; and the effect of applying MMA at inference time to an already-trained causal model is never explored, which would have been an easy and informative experiment.

Some reported results raise concerns: DOT performs dramatically worse than even the conventional baseline on MMB (43.8 vs 64.9), which is anomalous and unexplained; Table 8 reports AKI-4B RR as '0.65' inconsistent with the percentage scale of the table; and state-of-the-art comparisons in Table 2 mix leaderboard numbers, official-paper numbers, and dev-set evaluations (MMBdev) of different training data and pipelines, weakening the 'superior to models of similar size' claim.

Qualitative evidence is limited to a handful of cherry-picked examples (Figure 1 is a single image), and the hallucination-focused evaluation is essentially limited to POPE; no dedicated hallucination benchmarks or human evaluation are provided despite hallucination mitigation being the central motivation.
Reproducibility is weakened by the code link in the abstract being broken/absent and the AKI-4B release only promised for the future.

strengths: The core idea is simple, cheap, and well-motivated: unlocking the causal attention mask so that image tokens can attend to the question tokens (modality-mutual attention, MMA) requires no additional parameters or training time, and is trivially integrable into existing MLLM training pipelines.

The paper is commendably rigorous about apples-to-apples comparisons: all methods (standard I&T pipeline, CCA, dual-order training variants, MMA) are trained from scratch with identical data, model components, schedules, and evaluation protocol, which is stronger evidence than the common practice of comparing to third-party reported numbers.

The dual-order training (DOT) study is a useful contribution in its own right: it both validates the importance of cross-modal information flow and shows that naive order-augmented training is costly (2x per stage, factorial in modalities) and often harmful, which strengthens the case for a mask-level intervention.

Evaluation breadth is good: 12 benchmarks spanning general, knowledge, and vision-centric categories, with detailed per-category breakdowns in the appendix, official/pinned evaluation toolkits (VLMEvalKit, official CV-Bench code), greedy decoding for consistency, and detailed hyperparameters and prompt templates supporting reproducibility.

The limitation section is honest and technically substantive: it correctly identifies that naively applying MMA in the pretraining stage causes information leakage through the image-to-future-text attention path, and the choice to restrict MMA to SFT is explained rather than hidden.

The generalized mask formulation (Eq. 6) is a sensible step toward interleaved/multi-modal extensions, and the paper openly reports where AKI-4B loses to baselines (e.g., Qwen2-VL on MM-Bench, MathVista, MM-Vet categories).
weaknesses: Originality is overstated. The claim that revisiting causal attention for multimodal inputs is 'fundamental yet unexplored' ignores a line of closely related work on non-causal/prefix attention over image tokens (e.g., UniLM-style prefix-LM masks, MM1's ablations of bidirectional attention over image tokens and input ordering, and prefix/bidirectional attention in early fusion models). The related work discusses CCA but not this broader family, so the novelty amounts to a specific mask configuration (image attends to question tokens) rather than an unexplored perspective.

The evaluation lacks statistical rigor: all results appear to be single runs with no seeds, variance, or significance testing. This matters because several gains are small (POPE overall 82.7 for MMA vs. 81.9 for CCA and 82.7 for DOT; CV-Bench2D shows a decrease, marked '-') while others are implausibly large (MME-C +29.5%; text translation jumping 47.5 -> 92.5 -> 140 across models), and no mechanism or analysis is offered to explain the extreme values.

There is no ablation isolating the source of the improvement. The paper attributes gains to 'cross-modal information flow,' but there is no control experiment (e.g., attention to randomly sampled text tokens, or to instruction tokens only vs. full question) and no attention analysis/visualization confirming that image tokens actually use question information. The theoretical justification for why seeing the question reduces object hallucination is asserted rather than demonstrated.

The claimed generality ('generic, scalable to other modalities, interleaved data') is not empirically supported: no experiments on a second LLM backbone, a second vision encoder, multiple images, or non-vision modalities are provided, and the AKI-4B model explicitly does not support interleaved inputs.

There are presentation/data inconsistencies that undermine confidence: e.g., in Table 8 the AKI-4B RR entry is '0.65' (evidently inconsistent with percentages elsewhere); Table 7 shows MMA (Ours) at 1344.9 while Table 1 reports 1363.7 for MMA on MME-P; the DOT method degrades catastrophically on MMB (43.8 vs. 64.9 for the baseline) with no convincing explanation; the improvement row of Table 1 leaves CV-Bench2D as '-' despite CCA being worse than the base pipeline there.

The state-of-the-art comparison in Section 4.3 is somewhat misleading in framing: AKI-4B is compared against two older 7B models (LLaVA-1.5-7B, Honeybee) for the 'outperforms 7B models' claim, while several open-source 3B-class competitors (Qwen2-VL-2B, BLIP-3-4B, Phi-3-Vision) beat AKI-4B on key knowledge and vision-centric benchmarks. The headline '+7.2% average' is computed only against the CCA re-implementation, not against the field.

Evidence for the motivating claim (mitigating vision-language misalignment/hallucination) is comparatively thin: POPE gains over CCA are marginal (+0.8 overall), and the strongest evidence is anecdotal (Figures 1, 8-11 plus MME-C), which is fragile given benchmark-specific quirks in MME.

Because MMA is applied only at SFT (due to the acknowledged leakage issue at pretraining), the method's applicability to pretraining-time scaling - arguably where architecture changes matter most - remains unresolved, limiting the significance of the 'fundamental architecture' framing.
